about.title: Bell Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Bell is a dense, mixed residential and commercial city in Los Angeles County, and its shops, apartment buildings, and public sidewalks see steady foot traffic every day. When a property owner or manager lets a spill, broken step, cracked pavement, or poor lighting go unaddressed, the result can be a fall that leaves someone with real injuries and mounting medical bills. California law doesn't make every fall the property owner's fault — you generally have to show they knew, or should have known, about the hazard and failed to fix it or warn you. That's why documentation matters so much: photos of the hazard, witness names, and store surveillance footage can make or break a claim. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves. We're a free service that listens to what happened and connects you with an independent attorney in our network who takes premises liability cases on contingency, meaning there's no fee unless they recover money for you.

whyChoose.title: What Matters Most in a Bell Premises Case

items.title: Proving the Property Owner Knew
items.desc: California requires showing the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix or warn about it. An attorney knows how to gather maintenance logs, complaint records, and inspection history to build that case.

items.title: Acting Before Video Disappears
items.desc: Many Bell businesses only retain surveillance footage for a short window before it's overwritten. An attorney can send a preservation request quickly so critical video isn't lost.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're partly blamed for not seeing a hazard, you may still recover a reduced amount. An attorney can help make sure your share of fault isn't overstated by an insurer.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Bell?
items.answer: In most cases, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a public entity, such as a city building or school, the deadline is much shorter and requires an early claim filing. It's best to have this reviewed quickly so you don't lose your options.

items.question: What if I fell at a store on Florence Avenue or Gage Avenue and no one else saw it happen?
items.answer: You're not out of luck if there were no witnesses. Store surveillance cameras, incident reports, and even the condition of your clothing or shoes afterward can help support your claim. An attorney can request footage and records before they're deleted or discarded.

items.question: Will I still get compensation if I was partly at fault for not noticing the hazard?
items.answer: Possibly, yes. California follows a pure comparative fault rule, which means your compensation can be reduced by your percentage of fault rather than eliminated entirely. An attorney can help gather evidence to keep that percentage as accurate and low as the facts support.
